result.summary: After an argument summarizing the whole play, Orestes arrives at his father Agamemnon's tomb with Pylades, leaves a lock of hair, and hides when he sees Electra and a chorus of women bringing libations. Sent by Clytaemestra after a frightening dream, the women lament, and Electra, unsure how to pray, takes their advice and prays for Orestes' return and for vengeance.

scenes.title: Setting and argument of the play
scenes.summary: Details of staging and date, followed by a summary of the plot: Clytaemestra's dream, Orestes' return, the vengeance and his madness.

scenes.title: Orestes at his father's tomb
scenes.summary: Orestes prays to Hermes, offers two locks of hair, and sees mourning women led by Electra. He withdraws with Pylades to watch.
scenes.stakes: Orestes risks being discovered while seeking vengeance for his father's murder.

scenes.title: The chorus's lament
scenes.summary: The women describe being sent with libations after the queen's terrifying dream, and mourn the ruined house and the power of blood-guilt.
scenes.stakes: The women fear the consequences of carrying out a hated, godless rite under a master they resent.

scenes.title: Electra's prayer and libation
scenes.summary: Electra asks the women how to pray; they urge her to ask for an avenger. She invokes Hermes, Earth and her father, prays for Orestes, and pours the libations.
scenes.stakes: Electra, enslaved and dispossessed, seeks justice for her father and the return of Orestes.

notable_quotes.reason: Chorus asks what can atone for spilled blood, a key theme of the trilogy.
Expresses the law of blood vengeance: life for life.

analysis.text: The opening sets the cycle of blood vengeance: spilled blood cannot be cleansed, and the murdered demand retribution.
The play was staged in 458 B.C. at the City Dionysia as the middle part of the Oresteia trilogy.

legacy.text: The recognition scene that follows, with a lock of hair, was parodied by Euripides in his Electra and influenced later drama.

fun_facts.text: The Oresteia is the only surviving complete Greek tragic trilogy.

language_notes.text: "Wroth" is an archaic word for angry; "baleful" means threatening harm or evil.
"Noxious" means harmful; "clotted" describes blood thickened into lumps.
"If haply she might placate" means "in case she might perhaps appease." "Nether powers" are the gods and spirits of the underworld.
Offering a lock of hair was a mourning custom, and it later serves as a token by which Electra recognizes her brother.
The Erinyes are the Furies, avenging spirits who pursue those who shed kindred blood. Here they would act for his murdered father.
"Powers that are thy sire's": Hermes guards the authority once held by his father Zeus, and here also the dead below; the phrase is ambiguous and debated.
The broken-off ending (". . .") marks a gap in the surviving text; the lines are damaged or missing.
Inachus is the river god of Argos. Offering a lock of hair to a local river was a custom of thanks for a youth's upbringing.
"Sable weeds" means black mourning clothes; "weeds" is an old word for garments.
"Libations" are liquids poured out as offerings to the dead or the gods.
"Of a surety" means for certain; "import" here means signify or mean.
Libations are liquid offerings, here poured at Agamemnon's tomb to appease the dead.
"Rendings" means the tearing of garments in grief; the clause says the robe is torn because of sorrows far from any joy.
"The inspiring power who divines for the house" is the dream-spirit or prophetic force that sends warnings to the household in sleep.
"Graceless grace" is a paradox: an offering meant as a favor, but given without goodwill and only out of fear.
The speaker is a captive, probably taken after the fall of Troy, so her "city" is Troy and her slavery follows its capture.
"Touching this" means "concerning this"; Electra asks the women for advice about how to word her prayer.
"Forsooth" is archaic and sarcastic: she mocks the usual formula of asking the dead to repay the givers, since the givers are evil.
Refers to the custom of casting away the purification refuse and the vessel without looking back, so the polluting evil is not carried home.
"Fated hour" means death, which comes to free and enslaved alike; she tells the women to speak without fear.
The Chorus advises her to pray for herself and for all enemies of Aegisthus, so that the prayer also asks for vengeance.
"Life for life" expresses the law of blood retaliation: a killer must pay with his own death.
"Nether Hermes": Hermes in his role as guide of souls to the underworld, here asked to carry her prayer to the dead.
"Lustral offerings" are liquids poured in purification or ritual; here the libations for the dead Agamemnon.
"Bartered away": Clytemnestra is said to have sold her children, taking Aegisthus in exchange, as though they were goods.
"Wanton bravely in the winnings of thy toil" means they revel splendidly in wealth Agamemnon earned by his labors.
"Crown them with flowers of lamentation" asks the Chorus to follow the libation with a funeral song, as if with garlands.

context_notes.text: The "heroic age" is the legendary era of the Trojan War and its aftermath, when the story is set.
The City Dionysia was Athens' spring festival of Dionysus, where tragedies were performed in competition.
Pylades is Orestes' devoted friend and cousin, raised with him in Phocis; he is a mostly silent companion in the play.
Agamemnon was killed by Clytaemestra, who entangled him in a robe or net while he bathed after returning from Troy.
Hermes, as guide of souls, was invoked as a go-between with the dead. Orestes returns after years of exile to avenge Agamemnon.
Agamemnon was murdered by his wife Clytemnestra and Aegisthus on his return from Troy, and buried without proper rites; Orestes was away in exile.
Electra is Orestes' sister, who has remained in the house under Clytemnestra's rule and mourns their father.
Clytemnestra dreamed of terror after killing Agamemnon; this nightmare prompts her to send offerings to his grave.
Interpreters of dreams and portents were consulted in Greek households; here they read the dream as anger from the murdered dead.
The "violation of a bridal bower" refers to Clytemnestra's adultery and the crime against her husband's marriage bed.
The Chorus are captive serving women sent by Clytemnestra with Electra to the tomb of Agamemnon after her frightening dream.
Electra's "mother" Clytemnestra murdered her husband Agamemnon, so Electra cannot honestly call the offerings a wife's gift.
Aegisthus is Clytemnestra's lover and co-murderer of Agamemnon, now ruling Argos.
Orestes, Electra's brother, was sent away as a child and lives in exile; the women hope for his return as avenger.
Hermes was herald of the gods and guide of the dead, so he links the living world with the world below.
Aegisthus was Clytemnestra's lover and co-murderer of Agamemnon; he now rules Argos with her.
Electra seeks an avenger for Agamemnon; the audience understands this to mean Orestes, whose return she has just prayed for.

literary_notes.text: The serpent suckled at her breast symbolizes Orestes, whom she bore and who will draw her blood in vengeance.
Electra's slave-like treatment establishes her suffering and her loyalty to her father's memory.
The closing madness hints at the sequel, in which the Furies pursue Orestes (the next play, the Eumenides).
His guilt at missing the funeral reveals Orestes' sense of filial duty and motivates the vengeance.
A string of questions shows Orestes' sudden surprise and builds suspense as he works out who the mourners are.
Orestes turns to Zeus in direct prayer, stating the avenging purpose that drives the play.
Nail-marks are called "furrows" and the heart "fed" with lamentation, turning grief into plowing and nourishment.
Darkness enshrouding the house stands for the moral and political gloom that follows the king's murder.
The chorus says men treat Success as more than God, implying such worship is misplaced as Justice still watches.
Justice is imagined as a watchful figure with a balanced scale who delivers punishment at different times in life.
Even every stream flowing together could not wash away the stain, stressing how permanent blood-guilt is.
Electra's string of questions shows her perplexity and moral conflict about praying piously for a father whose murderers sent the gift.
The customary prayer, that the givers be repaid with good, becomes bitterly ironic because the givers are the murderers.
Electra treats the servants as friends and allies, showing shared hatred and her isolation within her own household.
Electra's moral scruple about praying for vengeance shows her piety and hesitation, which the Chorus quickly overrides.
Electra addresses Hermes and Earth directly, as if present, to carry her appeal to the dead.
Her slavery and Orestes' exile are set against the killers' proud enjoyment, sharpening the injustice she describes.
Justice crowned with victory invokes the play's recurring theme that blood demands blood under divine sanction.
